\section[punhā]{\mr{पुन्हा} (punhā) — \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C04-punha}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 4 gave you the goodbye \emph{yeto} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}). Now the explicit word for \textbf{again}, to build the warm \textquotedblleft{}see you again.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{पु}} (\emph{pu}) + \textbf{\mr{न्हा}} (\emph{nhā}, the \mr{न} \emph{na} joined by a \emph{halant} to \mr{ह} \emph{ha} with the long-\emph{ā} stroke) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{पुन्हा}} \emph{punhā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{पुन्हा}} (\emph{punhā}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{पुनर्}} (\emph{punar}, \textquotedblleft{}again, back\textquotedblright{}). That \emph{punar} is a genuine Indo-European cousin of Latin \textbf{re-} in the sense of \textquotedblleft{}back/again,\textquotedblright{} and it echoes in Hindi \emph{phir} and the \emph{puna-} of \emph{punarjanma} (\textquotedblleft{}rebirth\textquotedblright{}). To say a thing \emph{punhā} is to send it round once more.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Marathi's goodbyes lean on \emph{again} and \emph{meet} rather than on \emph{farewell} — the parting is framed as a \textbf{return}, never an ending. This word is the hinge of that idea.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}punhā\textquotedblright{} — again
  \item its Sanskrit source (\emph{punar}) and the \emph{punarjanma} echo
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{punhā} mean, and from what Sanskrit word? (\textquotedblleft{}Again\textquotedblright{}; from \emph{punar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bheṭū]{\mr{भेटू} (bheṭū) — \textquotedblleft{}(let's / we'll) meet\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C04-bhetu}



\begin{quote}
The other half of the goodbye: \textbf{meet}. You already brushed past it in \emph{bheṭūn ānand jhālā} (\textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{भे}} (\emph{bhe}) + \textbf{\mr{टू}} (\emph{ṭū}, the retroflex \mr{ट} \emph{ṭa} with the long-\emph{u} stroke) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{भेटू}} \emph{bheṭū}. Note the \textbf{retroflex \mr{ट}} (\emph{ṭa}) — the tongue curls back to the roof of the mouth.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{भेटू}} (\emph{bheṭū}) is a form of the verb \textbf{\mr{भेटणे}} (\emph{bheṭṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{}). As \textbf{\mr{भेटू}} it means \textquotedblleft{}let's meet / (we) will meet\textquotedblright{} — the hopeful, forward-looking mood you want in a goodbye. It is a native Marathi verb (the \emph{bheṭ-} stem also gives \emph{bheṭ}, \textquotedblleft{}a meeting, a visit\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one verb, first-person-plural wish}]
\textbf{\mr{भेटू}} carries a built-in \textquotedblleft{}we/let's\textquotedblright{} — no separate word for \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{} is needed, the verb form says it. This is the same \textbf{-ū} ending you'll feel in other \textquotedblleft{}let's \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} verbs. Unlike the present tense (\emph{yeto/yete}), this future-wish form does \textbf{not} split by gender — men and women both say \emph{bheṭū}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bheṭū\textquotedblright{} — (we'll) meet
  \item the fuller verb it comes from (\emph{bheṭṇe}, to meet)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bheṭū} pack into one word? (\textquotedblleft{}(we/let's) will meet\textquotedblright{} — the \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{} lives in the verb ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[punhā bheṭū]{\mr{पुन्हा} \mr{भेटू} (punhā bheṭū) — \textquotedblleft{}see you again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C04-punha-bhetu}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the two atoms into the standard warm goodbye.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the phrase, assembled}
\textbf{\mr{पुन्हा}} (\emph{punhā}, again) + \textbf{\mr{भेटू}} (\emph{bheṭū}, we'll meet) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{पुन्हा} \mr{भेटू}} — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again.\textquotedblright{} Two words, and the whole promise of return is spoken.

This is the fuller, explicit twin of Chapter 4's \textbf{\mr{येतो}} (\emph{yeto}, \textquotedblleft{}I'll come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}). Both refuse a final \textquotedblleft{}farewell\textquotedblright{}: one says \emph{I'll come back}, the other \emph{we'll meet again} — the subcontinent's shared goodbye-as-promise (Hindi \emph{phir milenge}, Bengali \emph{āshi}, Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}).

\begin{culture}
You can stack them for warmth: \textbf{\mr{येतो}, \mr{पुन्हा} \mr{भेटू}} (\emph{yeto, punhā bheṭū}) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll be going; we'll meet again.\textquotedblright{} Neither word contains \textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{}; the parting is all return.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}punhā bheṭū\textquotedblright{} — see you again
  \item it stacked with the Chapter-1 goodbye (\emph{yeto, punhā bheṭū})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{punhā bheṭū} literally promise? (\textquotedblleft{}We'll meet \textbf{again}\textquotedblright{} — return, not farewell.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[udyā bheṭū]{\mr{उद्या} \mr{भेटू} (udyā bheṭū) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C04-udya-bhetu}



\begin{quote}
Swap \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} for \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} and you have a dated goodbye.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{उ}} (\emph{u}, standalone vowel) + \textbf{\mr{द्या}} (\emph{dyā}, \mr{द} \emph{da} joined by a \emph{halant} to \mr{य} \emph{ya} with the long-\emph{ā} stroke) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{उद्या}} \emph{udyā}.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the phrase, assembled}
\textbf{\mr{उद्या}} (\emph{udyā}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\mr{भेटू}} (\emph{bheṭū}, we'll meet) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{उद्या} \mr{भेटू}} — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{\mr{उद्या}} comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{श्वः}} (\emph{śvaḥ}) by way of a later \emph{udya-}; unlike Hindi's \emph{kal} (which means \emph{both} tomorrow and yesterday), Marathi keeps \textbf{tomorrow} and \textbf{yesterday} as two distinct words — \emph{udyā} (tomorrow) vs. \textbf{\mr{काल}} (\emph{kāl}, yesterday). No ambiguity about which way time is pointing.

\begin{culture}
Because \emph{bheṭū} already carries the future wish, you simply front it with \emph{when}: \emph{udyā bheṭū} (tomorrow), \emph{punhā bheṭū} (again). The verb does the tense; the first word sets the day.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}udyā bheṭū\textquotedblright{} — see you tomorrow
  \item the tomorrow/yesterday pair Marathi keeps apart (\emph{udyā / kāl})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Marathi's \emph{udyā} differ from Hindi's \emph{kal}? (\emph{udyā} is only \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}; Marathi uses a separate word \emph{kāl} for \textquotedblleft{}yesterday.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāḷjī ghyā]{\mr{काळजी} \mr{घ्या} (kāḷjī ghyā) — \textquotedblleft{}take care\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C04-kalji-ghya}



\begin{quote}
One last, tender goodbye — the Marathi \textquotedblleft{}take care,\textquotedblright{} and with it a letter unique to Marathi's corner of Devanagari.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{काळजी}} carries the letter \textbf{\mr{ळ}} (\emph{ḷa}) — a \textbf{retroflex \textquotedblleft{}l,\textquotedblright{}} the tongue curled back. Standard Hindi dropped this sound; Marathi (like the Dravidian south and Gujarati) keeps it, and it appears in many everyday Marathi words. \textbf{\mr{का}} + \textbf{\mr{ळ}} + \textbf{\mr{जी}} $\to$ \emph{kāḷjī}. Then \textbf{\mr{घ्या}} (\emph{ghyā}, \textquotedblleft{}take,\textquotedblright{} respectful).

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the phrase, assembled}
\textbf{\mr{काळजी}} (\emph{kāḷjī}, \textquotedblleft{}care, concern\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\mr{घ्या}} (\emph{ghyā}, \textquotedblleft{}take,\textquotedblright{} the respectful imperative) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{काळजी} \mr{घ्या}} — \textquotedblleft{}take care.\textquotedblright{} To a friend, the familiar imperative: \textbf{\mr{काळजी} \mr{घे}} (\emph{kāḷjī ghe}).

\begin{culture}
Where \emph{punhā bheṭū} looks ahead to the next meeting, \emph{kāḷjī ghyā} looks after the person in between — \textquotedblleft{}mind yourself until then.\textquotedblright{} The respectful \textbf{\mr{घ्या}} (\emph{ghyā}) matches the \textbf{\mr{तुम्ही}} register from Chapter 9; the familiar \textbf{\mr{घे}} (\emph{ghe}) matches \textbf{\mr{तू}}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kāḷjī ghyā\textquotedblright{} (respectful) / \textquotedblleft{}kāḷjī ghe\textquotedblright{} (to a friend)
  \item the retroflex \mr{ळ} (\emph{ḷa}) Marathi keeps that Hindi lost
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which special Marathi letter sits in \emph{kāḷjī}, and who else keeps it? (The retroflex \textbf{\mr{ळ}} \emph{ḷa}; also kept by the Dravidian languages and Gujarati.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 11 recap — farewells}

\label{lesson:MR-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
The parting words, together — none of them a bare \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the farewells}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Marathi} & \textbf{Say it} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\mr{येतो} / \mr{येते}. & \emph{yeto / yete.} & I'll be going. (\textquotedblleft{}I come again\textquotedblright{}) \\
\mr{पुन्हा} \mr{भेटू}. & \emph{punhā bheṭū.} & See you again. \\
\mr{उद्या} \mr{भेटू}. & \emph{udyā bheṭū.} & See you tomorrow. \\
\mr{काळजी} \mr{घ्या}. & \emph{kāḷjī ghyā.} & Take care. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — atoms banked this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{पुन्हा}} (\emph{punhā}) — again; Sanskrit \emph{punar}.
  \item \textbf{\mr{भेटू}} (\emph{bheṭū}) — (we'll) meet; the \textquotedblleft{}we\textquotedblright{} lives in the verb; from \emph{bheṭṇe}.
  \item \textbf{\mr{उद्या}} (\emph{udyā}) — tomorrow (distinct from \emph{kāl}, yesterday).
  \item \textbf{\mr{काळजी} \mr{घ्या}} (\emph{kāḷjī ghyā}) — take care; the retroflex \textbf{\mr{ळ}} Marathi keeps.
  \item Register: \textbf{\mr{घ्या}} (\emph{ghyā}, respectful) vs \textbf{\mr{घे}} (\emph{ghe}, familiar) — the \emph{tumhī / tū} choice again.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all four farewells in a row
  \item a stacked goodbye — \emph{yeto, punhā bheṭū, kāḷjī ghyā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does every Marathi goodbye have in common? (None says \textquotedblleft{}farewell\textquotedblright{} — each is a \textbf{return} or a caring wish.) Next chapter: the first real verbs — \emph{mī marāṭhī bolto.}
\end{tcolorbox}
